Inverse kinematics of robot arms

Inverse kinematics (IK) is the opposite of forward kinematics: given a desired pose of the tool, find joint values ||(q||) that reach it. It is harder: the equations are nonlinear, and there may be several solutions, infinitely many, or none at all. This notebook solves it in three ways, using the MRPT Python wheel (pip install mrpt3) for the poses (mrpt.poses.CPose3D) and the forward kinematics (pose composition ||(\oplus||), the + operator), which checks every solution:
  1. Closed form for a planar arm with two links: two solutions.
  2. Kinematic decoupling for a 6-DOF arm with a spherical wrist: eight solutions.
  3. Numerical methods based on the Jacobian, which work for any robot: Jacobian transpose, pseudo-inverse and damped least squares.
The robots are described with Denavit-Hartenberg tables (see the DH parameters notebook).

1. Closed form: a planar arm with two links

The tool of a planar arm with links of lengths ||(l_1||) and ||(l_2||) is at ||[x = l_1 \cos\theta_1 + l_2 \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2), \qquad y = l_1 \sin\theta_1 + l_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2).||]Squaring and adding both equations removes ||(\theta_1||) (the law of cosines), and then ||(\theta_1||) follows from the angle to the target: ||[\cos\theta_2 = \frac{x^2 + y^2 - l_1^2 - l_2^2}{2\, l_1 l_2}, \qquad \theta_2 = \pm \arccos(\cos\theta_2), \qquad \theta_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x) - \operatorname{atan2}(l_2 \sin\theta_2,\; l_1 + l_2 \cos\theta_2).||]The sign of ||(\theta_2||) gives two solutions, elbow down and elbow up. They become one on the border of the workspace, an annulus of radii ||(|l_1 - l_2|||) and ||(l_1 + l_2||), and there is none outside it. Move the target around and out of reach.

2. Kinematic decoupling: a 6-DOF arm with a spherical wrist

Most industrial arms have a spherical wrist: the axes of the last three joints meet at one point, the wrist center ||(p_w||). Then the problem splits into two smaller ones (Pieper's method). The anthropomorphic arm used here has this DH table (lengths in meters):
Link ||(\theta_i||) ||(d_i||) ||(a_i||) ||(\alpha_i||)
1 ||(q_1||) 0.4 0 90°
2 ||(q_2||) 0 0.5 0
3 ||(q_3||) 0 0 90°
4 ||(q_4||) 0.5 0 -90°
5 ||(q_5||) 0 0 90°
6 ||(q_6||) 0.1 0 0
  1. Position. The tool lies ||(d_6||) along its approach axis ||(z_6||) from the wrist center, so ||(p_w = p_e - d_6\, z_6||), and ||(p_w||) only depends on ||(\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3||). Joint 1 turns the arm towards it: ||(\theta_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(p_{w,y}, p_{w,x})||), or that plus 180° (reaching backwards). In the vertical plane of the arm, the upper arm (||(a_2||)) and the forearm (||(d_4||)) are a planar 2R arm, solved as in section 1, with ||(\theta_3||) shifted 90° because the forearm lies along ||(z_3||).
  2. Orientation. With ||(\theta_{1,2,3}||) known, so is the rotation ||(R_0^3||) of frame 3, and the wrist must provide the rest: ||(R_3^6 = (R_0^3)^\top R_e||). The spherical wrist is a set of ||(ZYZ||) Euler angles:
||[R_3^6 = \begin{bmatrix} c_4 c_5 c_6 - s_4 s_6 & -c_4 c_5 s_6 - s_4 c_6 & c_4 s_5 \\ s_4 c_5 c_6 + c_4 s_6 & -s_4 c_5 s_6 + c_4 c_6 & s_4 s_5 \\ -s_5 c_6 & s_5 s_6 & c_5 \end{bmatrix} \;\Rightarrow\; \begin{aligned} \theta_5 &= \operatorname{atan2}\big(\pm\sqrt{r_{13}^2 + r_{23}^2},\, r_{33}\big) \\ \theta_4 &= \operatorname{atan2}(\pm r_{23}, \pm r_{13}) \\ \theta_6 &= \operatorname{atan2}(\pm r_{32}, \mp r_{31}) \end{aligned}||]Two choices for the shoulder, two for the elbow and two for the wrist: up to eight solutions for the same tool pose. Move the target and pick a solution to highlight. Near ||(\theta_5 = 0||) (a wrist singularity) only ||(\theta_4 + \theta_6||) is defined.

3. Numerical inverse kinematics

Closed forms only exist for some geometries. The general method is iterative: start at a guess ||(q_0||), measure the pose error ||(e(q) = \begin{bmatrix} p_d - p(q) \\ \log\big(R_d\, R(q)^\top\big) \end{bmatrix}||) (position, and the rotation vector of the remaining rotation) and move the joints to reduce it, using the Jacobian ||(J(q)||), which relates small joint motions to small tool motions:
Method Update ||(\Delta q||) Notes
Jacobian transpose ||(\alpha\, J^\top e||) gradient descent: cheap and stable, but slow
Pseudo-inverse (Newton-Raphson) ||(J^{+} e||) very fast near the solution; huge steps near singularities
Damped least squares (Levenberg-Marquardt) ||(J^\top (J J^\top + \lambda^2 I)^{-1} e||) a compromise; ||(\lambda||) limits the steps
Here it is applied to the UR5, whose wrist is not spherical. The initial guess decides which of its solutions is found. Things to try:
  • Change the initial guess and compare the final configurations.
  • Move the target out of reach (e.g. ||(x = -1||) m): the pseudo-inverse jumps around (the tool moves more than 1 m in some iterations), while damped least squares takes short steps and, with ||(\lambda \approx 0.2||), settles at the closest pose.
  • Set ||(\lambda = 0||): damped least squares becomes the pseudo-inverse.
